newsitem.title: JAPAN: ADB gropes forward to the 21st century.
newsitem.headline: ADB gropes forward to the 21st century.

text.p: The Asian Development Bank, groping for a new role in a region struggling to keep up its economic miracle, opens its annual meeting on Sunday hoping to find the way into the 21st century.

Back in Japan for the third time for a gathering sometimes scorned as a big cocktail party, the ADB lived up to its name as banker to the world's fastest growing region by attracting top business leaders as well as Asian policy makers.

But 30 years since its inception as a quasi-government provider for poor nations, the changing economic fortunes of most of Asia has left the bank uncertain about its future in a region where private capital now rules.

"We must zero in on what we are best at. In other words, we must leave to private investors what they are willing -- and able -- to do," ADB governor Mitsuo Sato said in a newspaper interview published on Saturday.
"The primary objective of the upcoming annual meeting is to bring home where our strengths lie," he told Japan's Asahi Evening newspaper.
"Increasingly we will be marginalised and dwarfed without finding our relevance in the new environment," Sato had said in a Reuter interview earlier in the week.
One suggestion of the way the bank should go is that it should encourage businessmen into areas where there are currently no profits by itself making the first few investments to make it attractive.
The bank could also advise governments on how to reform their economies, particularly the financial and capital markets.
Partly because of their own budgetary problems and also because private money is now flowing across the region, traditional donors are asking why they should hand out aid.
"Many donors are saying the bank should do without any new capital injection but borrowing countries have a different opinion," Sato said.
Unlike last year, when delegates from the 56 member nations haggled over how much money each should pay for aid, the agenda for this meeting is mainly about philosophical questions.

The bank, started at a time when the world was divided by ideological barriers and Asia's poorest nations were starved of capital, has found itself being pushed aside by the private capital flowing into the region.

In a sign of the times, eve-of-meeting gatherings which featured lavish business seminars and a reception attended by the Crown Prince and Princess of Japan, were mostly overshadowed by the previous day's action in foreign exchange markets.

Most reporters shunned the seminars, attended by financial policymakers and business leaders,to chase the Japanese finance minister and central bank governor for comment on Friday's drop in the dollar to under 120 yen.
At the main seminar, on Asian financial markets, policymakers spoke of the new challenge to the region -- not how to become wealthy, but how best to manage their wealth.

"While there have been periods of financial distress in individual banking systems in the region in the past years, such incidents have been far fewer and less severe than in other emerging markets," Hong Kong Monetary Authority chief executive Joseph Yam told the forum.

"The Asian economy has achieved a phenomenal success in the past several decades but we must stress better risk management and a more stable framework," said Toyoo Gyoten, former Japanese finance ministry official and chairman of the Washington, D.C.- based Institute of International Finance, which hosted the forum.
